cse-1995-b-63-b.approach: Read the 1s off the map and look for the largest wrap-around groups: the four corners form one quad and the four centre cells form another. Two quads cover all eight 1s, so the SOP has two terms.

steps.title: Corner quad
steps.body: Corners: $AB\in\{00,10\}$ and $CD\in\{00,10\}$. They are adjacent by wrap-around. Constant variables: $B=0$, $D=0$ ($A$, $C$ vary) $\Rightarrow \overline{B}\,\overline{D}$.

steps.title: Centre quad
steps.body: Centre: $AB\in\{01,11\}$, $CD\in\{01,11\}$. Constant: $B=1$, $D=1$ $\Rightarrow BD$.

steps.title: Minimal SOP
steps.body:
All 1s are covered by two essential prime implicants, so
$$F = BD + \overline{B}\,\overline{D} \;(= \overline{B \oplus D})$$

pitfalls: Missing the corner wrap-around and writing four 2-cell terms instead of one quad.
Reading the map with rows/columns swapped — here columns are AB and rows CD.
cse-1995-b-63-b.verification: F = 1 exactly when B = D; every listed 1-cell has B = D and every blank cell has B ≠ D.

cse-1995-b-64-a.approach: Trace the registers: B is a count (10), A the search key (05H), HL a pointer (1C40H). The subroutine compares A with memory at HL and returns as soon as they are equal — a linear search.

steps.title: Set-up
steps.body: `MVI B,0AH` → counter $B=10$; `MVI A,05H` → key $A=05H$; `LXI H,1C40H` → pointer $HL=1C40H$; then `CALL SUB`.

steps.title: Loop body
steps.body: `CMP M` computes $A-M[HL]$ and sets Z if they are equal. `RZ` returns immediately on a match. Otherwise `INX H` moves to the next byte, `DCR B` decrements the count, and `JNZ SUB` repeats while $B\ne0$.

steps.title: What it does
steps.body: It searches the 10 bytes at $1C40H$–$1C49H$ for the value $05H$. On a match it returns with HL pointing at the first location holding 05H; if no location matches it returns after 10 comparisons (via `RET`) and the program halts.

answer.value: Linear search: looks for the byte 05H in the 10 locations 1C40H–1C49H; stops with HL pointing to the first location containing 05H (or after all 10 if none does).

pitfalls: CMP M does not change A — it only sets flags.
RZ returns from SUB to the instruction after CALL (HLT), not to the start.
cse-1995-b-64-a.verification: Counted iterations: B = 0AH = 10 gives addresses 1C40H…1C49H before DCR B reaches 0.

animation.code:
MVI B, 0AH
MVI A, 05H
LXI H, 1C40H
CALL SUB
HLT
SUB: CMP M
RZ
INX H
DCR B
JNZ SUB
RET

cse-1995-b-64-b.approach: The first two instructions are immediate loads, so the initial register contents are just their operands. The printed "U" is a misprint for B — the only other register the program loads.

steps.title: Immediate loads
steps.body: `MVI B,0AH` puts $0AH$ ($=10$) in B; `MVI A,05H` puts $05H$ in A.

steps.title: Roles
steps.body: A holds the byte being searched for and B is the loop counter (10 locations).

pitfalls: Reading 0AH as decimal 0A or as the letter O; it is hexadecimal 0A = 10.
cse-1995-b-64-b.verification: Matches the loop: 10 decrements of B take it from 0AH to 0.

cse-1995-b-64-c.approach: HL is advanced by INX H only after a failed comparison, and RZ returns before that increment on a match. So HL ends at the matching address, or one past the last searched address if nothing matched.

steps.title: Match case
steps.body: If $M[1C40H+k]=05H$ for the first time at $k$ ($0\le k\le9$), `CMP M` sets Z and `RZ` returns before `INX H`. So $HL = 1C40H + k$, the address of the first 05H.

steps.title: No-match case
steps.body:
Each failed pass does `INX H`. After 10 passes $B=0$, `JNZ` falls through to `RET` and
$$HL = 1C40H + 0AH = 1C4AH.$$

answer.value: HL = address of the first location in 1C40H–1C49H that contains 05H; HL = 1C4AH if none of them does.

pitfalls: Saying 1C49H for the no-match case — INX H runs once more after the last comparison.
cse-1995-b-64-c.verification: Traced with no match: HL takes 1C40H…1C49H at the 10 compares and is incremented 10 times in total → 1C4AH.

cse-1995-b-65-a-i.approach: A start-stop frame is: start bit 0, the data bits, the parity bit, then the stop bit 1. Odd parity makes the total count of 1s (data + parity) odd.

steps.title: Parity bit
steps.body: Data `0110101` has $0+1+1+0+1+0+1 = 4$ ones (even). For odd parity the parity bit must be **1** (total 5).

steps.title: Assemble the frame
steps.body:
| start | data (7) | parity | stop |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0110101 | 1 | 1 |

Bit stream: **0 0110101 1 1** — 10 bits per character.

pitfalls: Using even parity (would give parity 0).
Forgetting the start bit — the frame is 10 bits, not 9.
cse-1995-b-65-a-i.verification: Ones in data + parity = 4 + 1 = 5, which is odd.

cse-1995-b-65-a-ii.approach: Each character occupies a full 10-bit frame (1 start + 7 data + 1 parity + 1 stop), so divide the line rate by 10.

steps.title: Strings per second
steps.body: $$\frac{1200\ \text{bits/s}}{10\ \text{bits/string}} = 120\ \text{strings/s}$$

pitfalls: Dividing by 7 (data bits only) gives 171, ignoring the framing bits.

cse-1995-b-65-b.approach: In graphics mode the buffer stores one bit per pixel, so find the pixel resolution from the text format and the character cell size.

steps.title: Resolution
steps.body: Width $= 80 \times 9 = 720$ pixels; height $= 25 \times 12 = 300$ pixels.

steps.title: Buffer size
steps.body: $$720 \times 300 \times 1\ \text{bit} = 216000\ \text{bits} = \frac{216000}{8} = 27000\ \text{bytes} \approx 26.4\ \text{KB}$$

pitfalls: Giving the text-mode size (80 × 25 = 2000 characters) instead of the graphics-mode pixel count.

cse-1995-b-66.approach: The range −8…+7 is exactly 4-bit two's complement, whose pattern for negative N equals the unsigned value N + 2⁴. After that the loop is the usual repeated-division conversion, writing each remainder as a decimal digit.

steps.title: Expression A
steps.body: For $-8\le N\le -1$, the 4-bit two's complement code of $N$ is the unsigned number $2^4+N$. So $A = N + 16$ (giving $8\ldots15$, i.e. `1000`…`1111`).

steps.title: Expressions B and C
steps.body: Each pass takes the lowest bit `REM := N mod 2`, places it at the current decimal position: $B = \text{REM}$, then drops that bit: $C = N \text{ div } 2$.

answer.value: A = N + 16, B = REM, C = N div 2

pitfalls: Using A = −N or abs(N) gives the magnitude, not the two's complement code.
Writing C = N / 2 — Pascal "/" is real division; integer division is div.
cse-1995-b-66.verification: N = −8 → 8 → 1000 and N = −1 → 15 → 1111, both correct 4-bit codes; positive N skips A.

animation.caption: Completed loop

cse-1995-b-67.approach: Each semaphore starts at 0 and is used by exactly one V and one P, so V(x) after Si and P(x) before Sj means Si must precede Sj: one edge per semaphore.

steps.title: Edge rule
steps.body: A semaphore initialised to 0 makes `P(x)` wait until some process does `V(x)`. So "Si; V(x)" in one block and "P(x); Sj" in another gives the edge $S_i \to S_j$.

scene.caption: Edges out of S1, S2, S3

steps.title: Precedence graph
steps.body: S1 forks into the S2 branch (S2 → S4, S5 → join at S7) and the S3 branch (S3 → S6 → S8, plus S3 → S8 directly). S7 and S8 both feed S9.

pitfalls: Omitting S3→S8 (semaphore h) because S3 already reaches S8 through S6 — the graph drawn from the code has it.
cse-1995-b-67.verification: Eleven semaphores a–k used, eleven edges drawn; every Si except S1 has at least one incoming edge.

cse-1995-b-68.approach: Add up |current − next| for the order each algorithm visits. FCFS keeps the queue order; SSTF always moves to the nearest pending track.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: SSTF needs 85 tracks against 204 for FCFS, so **SSTF** requires less head movement.

answer.value: SSTF needs less: FCFS = 204 tracks, SSTF = 85 tracks

pitfalls: From 75, SSTF goes to 23 (distance 52) before 10 (65), not the other way.

cse-1995-b-69-a.approach: Use the one-step subgroup test: a non-empty subset H is a subgroup if a, b ∈ H implies ab⁻¹ ∈ H. Both G₁ and G₂ pass it, so their intersection does too.

steps.title: Non-empty
steps.body: The identity $e$ of $G$ lies in every subgroup, so $e \in G_1 \cap G_2$.

steps.title: Closure under $ab^{-1}$
steps.body: Let $a, b \in G_1 \cap G_2$. Since $G_1$ is a subgroup, $ab^{-1} \in G_1$; since $G_2$ is a subgroup, $ab^{-1} \in G_2$. Hence $ab^{-1} \in G_1 \cap G_2$.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: By the one-step test, $G_1 \cap G_2$ is a subgroup of $G$. (The same argument works for any family of subgroups.)

answer.value: $G_1 \cap G_2$ is a subgroup: it contains $e$, and $a,b \in G_1\cap G_2 \Rightarrow ab^{-1} \in G_1$ and $\in G_2$.

pitfalls: Forgetting to show the set is non-empty.

cse-1995-b-69-b.approach: Give a counterexample. G₁ ∪ G₂ is a subgroup only when one subgroup contains the other; two subgroups of ℤ like 2ℤ and 3ℤ break closure.

steps.title: Counterexample
steps.body: In $(\mathbb{Z}, +)$ take $G_1 = 2\mathbb{Z}$, $G_2 = 3\mathbb{Z}$. Then $2, 3 \in G_1 \cup G_2$ but $2 + 3 = 5$ is divisible by neither 2 nor 3, so $5 \notin G_1 \cup G_2$. Closure fails.

steps.title: General fact
steps.body: If $a \in G_1\setminus G_2$ and $b \in G_2 \setminus G_1$, then $ab \in G_1$ would give $b = a^{-1}(ab) \in G_1$, and $ab \in G_2$ would give $a \in G_2$ — both false. So $G_1 \cup G_2$ is a subgroup **iff** $G_1 \subseteq G_2$ or $G_2 \subseteq G_1$.

answer.value: No. E.g. 2ℤ ∪ 3ℤ in (ℤ,+): 2 + 3 = 5 is not in the union. It is a subgroup only when one of G₁, G₂ contains the other.

pitfalls: Answering "never" — it is a subgroup when one contains the other (e.g. G₁ = G₂).

cse-1995-b-70.approach: Run Kruskal's algorithm and watch for ties: a tie between edges that could both be the next safe edge gives alternative MSTs. Here the only tie that matters is the two weight-4 edges into D.

steps.title: Forced edges
steps.body: Sorted: AB 2, AE 3, BC 3, BD 4, CD 4, ED 5. Take AB (2), AE (3), BC (3) — no cycles. Every MST must contain them: they are the strictly lightest ways to attach E and C.

steps.title: Connect D
steps.body: Component {A,B,C,E}; D is reached by BD (4), CD (4) or ED (5). The minimum is 4, achieved by **two** edges, and adding either closes no cycle. ED (5) is never chosen.

steps.title: The two MSTs
steps.body:
- **T₁** = {AB, AE, BC, BD}, weight $2+3+3+4 = 12$
- **T₂** = {AB, AE, BC, CD}, weight $2+3+3+4 = 12$

So the graph has **2** minimum spanning trees.

scene.caption: T₁ (T₂ uses CD instead of BD)

answer.value: 2 MSTs, each of weight 12: {AB, AE, BC, BD} and {AB, AE, BC, CD}

pitfalls: Counting the tie AE = BC = 3 as extra MSTs — both are needed, so it creates no alternative.
cse-1995-b-70.verification: Spanning trees avoiding both BD and CD must use ED (5) and weigh ≥ 13 > 12, so only these two achieve 12.

cse-1995-b-71.approach: Standard induction: check n = 5, then show 2^{k+1} = 2·2^k > 2k² and that 2k² ≥ (k+1)² once k ≥ 3.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: By induction, $2^n > n^2$ for all integers $n \ge 5$.

answer.value: Base n = 5: 32 > 25. If 2^k > k² (k ≥ 5) then 2^{k+1} > 2k² = (k+1)² + (k−1)² − 2 > (k+1)². Hence 2^n > n² for all n ≥ 5.

pitfalls: The claim fails for n = 2, 3, 4 (4 = 4, 8 < 9, 16 = 16), so the base case must be 5.

cse-1995-b-72.approach: Use the handshaking lemma: the degree sum is 2|E|, an even number. Split it into even-degree and odd-degree vertices; the odd part must be even, which needs an even number of odd terms.

steps.title: Handshaking lemma
steps.body: Each edge adds 1 to the degree of each endpoint (a loop adds 2 to one vertex), so $\sum_{v} \deg(v) = 2|E|$, which is even.

steps.title: Split the sum
steps.body:
Let $V_e$, $V_o$ be the even- and odd-degree vertices:
$$\sum_{v\in V_o}\deg(v) = 2|E| - \sum_{v\in V_e}\deg(v).$$
The right side is even minus even, so it is even.

steps.title: Count odd terms
steps.body: A sum of odd numbers is even only if it has an even number of terms. Hence $|V_o|$ is even.

answer.value: Σdeg(v) = 2|E| is even; the even-degree vertices contribute an even amount, so the odd degrees sum to an even number, which forces an even count of odd-degree vertices.

pitfalls: Asserting the conclusion without the "sum of odd numbers" parity step.

cse-1995-b-73-a.approach: Complete the square (or set the derivative to zero): the quadratic opens upward, so its vertex gives the minimum.

steps.title: Minimum
steps.body: $2(x-1)^2 \ge 0$, with equality at $x = 1$, so the minimum value is **1**. (Check: $f'(x) = 4x - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow x=1$, $f''=4>0$.)

pitfalls: Reporting x = 1 (the minimiser) instead of the minimum value 1 — here they coincide numerically, but the question asks for the value.

cse-1995-b-73-b.approach: 720 is divisible by 2, 3 and 5, so the count of integers coprime to 30 is exact: 720·(1−1/2)(1−1/3)(1−1/5). Inclusion–exclusion gives the same number.

steps.title: Complement
steps.body:
$$720 - 528 = 192$$
Check: $720\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac45 = 192$.

pitfalls: Forgetting to add back |A₃₀| = 24.
cse-1995-b-73-b.verification: Per block of 30 there are φ(30) = 8 such numbers; 720/30 = 24 blocks × 8 = 192.

cse-1995-b-74-a.approach: Find the candidate keys first (B never appears on a right side, so it is in every key). Then 3NF holds because the only non-key determinant C determines a prime attribute A, while BCNF fails because C is not a superkey.

steps.title: Keys
steps.body: $(AB)^+ = \{A,B,C\}$ and $(BC)^+ = \{B,C,A\}$; no single attribute is a key ($A^+=A$, $B^+=B$, $C^+=CA$). So the keys are $AB$ and $BC$, and **every** attribute is prime.

steps.title: 3NF
steps.body: For each FD $X\to Y$, 3NF needs $X$ a superkey **or** $Y$ prime. $AB\to C$: $AB$ is a key ✓. $C \to A$: $A$ is prime ✓. So R is in 3NF.

steps.title: Not BCNF
steps.body: BCNF needs every non-trivial determinant to be a superkey. $C^+ = \{C, A\} \ne R$, so $C\to A$ violates BCNF.

answer.value: Keys AB, BC ⇒ all attributes prime ⇒ 3NF; C → A has non-superkey C ⇒ not BCNF.

pitfalls: Claiming C → A violates 3NF — it does not, because A is prime.
cse-1995-b-74-a.verification: Classic example (e.g. Street, City → Zip; Zip → City) of 3NF-but-not-BCNF.

cse-1995-b-74-b.approach: B appears on no right side, so B is in every key; try B with one more attribute and check closures.

steps.title: B is mandatory
steps.body: No FD derives $B$, so every key contains $B$. $B^+ = \{B\}$ alone is not a key.

steps.title: Two-attribute keys
steps.body: $(AB)^+$: $AB\to C$ gives $\{A,B,C\}$ ✓. $(BC)^+$: $C\to A$ gives $\{A,B,C\}$ ✓. Both are minimal because $A^+ = \{A\}$, $B^+=\{B\}$, $C^+ = \{A,C\}$.

pitfalls: Listing only AB and missing BC.
cse-1995-b-74-b.verification: ABC is the only other superkey and it is not minimal.

cse-1995-b-75-a.approach: All publishers are stored in PUBLISHER, so just project its PNAME column.

steps.title: Project
steps.body: $$\pi_{\text{PNAME}}(\text{PUBLISHER})$$

steps.title: Why PUBLISHER
steps.body: Projecting BOOK would miss publishers that have not published any book yet.

pitfalls: Using π_PNAME(BOOK), which lists only publishers with at least one book.
cse-1995-b-75-a.verification: PNAME is the key of PUBLISHER, so the result has one row per publisher.

cse-1995-b-75-b.approach: Select the books of TECHNICAL PUBLISHERS, natural-join with AUTHOR on ANAME, and project back to the AUTHOR attributes.

steps.title: Books of the publisher
steps.body: $\sigma_{\text{PNAME}='\text{TECHNICAL PUBLISHERS}'}(\text{BOOK})$

steps.title: Join and project
steps.body:
$$\pi_{\text{ANAME, INSTITUTION, ACITY, AGE}}\big(\text{AUTHOR} \bowtie \sigma_{\text{PNAME}='\text{TECHNICAL PUBLISHERS}'}(\text{BOOK})\big)$$
The join is on the common attribute ANAME; projection removes TITLE and PNAME and duplicate rows.

pitfalls: Skipping the final projection returns TITLE and PNAME too, and repeats an author once per book.
cse-1995-b-75-b.verification: Equivalent: AUTHOR ⋉ σ(BOOK) (semijoin) gives the same tuples.

cse-1995-b-75-c.approach: Select publishers located in Madras, join with BOOK on PNAME to get their books, and project the author names.

steps.title: Madras publishers
steps.body: $\sigma_{\text{PCITY}='\text{Madras}'}(\text{PUBLISHER})$

steps.title: Join and project
steps.body:
$$\pi_{\text{ANAME}}\big(\text{BOOK} \bowtie \sigma_{\text{PCITY}='\text{Madras}'}(\text{PUBLISHER})\big)$$
The join is on PNAME; projection keeps each author once.

pitfalls: Selecting on ACITY = 'Madras' (the author's city) instead of the publisher's city PCITY.
cse-1995-b-75-c.verification: AUTHOR is not needed: ANAME is already in BOOK.
